topic: Peptides your body makes: orexin (hypocretin), the brain's own stay-awake peptide. Made by a small group of hypothalamic neurons; helps you stay awake and stabilises sleep-wake states (NINDS Narcolepsy page); 1998 two groups: de Lecea et al. named hypocretins (hypothalamic + secretin similarity), Sakurai et al. (Cell 1998) named orexins after Greek for appetite because they stimulated food intake in rats (Siegel, Cell 1999); 1999 Lin et al. (Cell): narcoleptic Doberman and Labrador dogs had deletions in Hcrtr2 (orexin receptor 2) gene; 2000 Thannickal et al. (Neuron): human narcoleptics had an 85-95% reduction in Hcrt neurons, on average only 7% left; narcolepsy: EDS in all, type 1 cataplexy triggered by strong emotions, caused by loss of hypocretin neurons (NINDS)

Lab notes · peptides your body makes

Your brain makes its own “stay awake” peptide.

Entry 1

Meet orexin.

Also called hypocretin. Made by a few nerve cells in the hypothalamus.

Job: help you stay awake.

1998

Two teams. One peptide.

Hypocretin = hypothalamus + secretin.

Orexin = Greek for appetite. It made rats eat more.

1999

The sleepy dogs.

Doberman and Labrador dogs with narcolepsy:

a broken gene for an orexin receptor.

2000

Then, human brains.

85–95%

of orexin cells lost in people with narcolepsy.

Result

Too little orexin:

Heavy daytime sleepiness.

Type 1: sudden muscle weakness with strong emotions, like laughing.

Don't lose this page

Save this for your neuro class.
